title.en: The Lost Daughter and the Reptile Husband
title.zh: 失蹤的女兒與蟒形丈夫

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Gone for good one day, the daughter of two hunter-brothers returns hooded and 'married to one not of human race,' nursing a biting, blood-lipped reptile in her amowt. Her brothers storm the great house in the valley, tear her offspring to pieces, and spear the house-sized husband as it comes in twined about her body — then warn her off her bad habits. But a black-streaked worm grows daily in her hand until she disappears again, the mother dying on the search, one brother's leg broken, and the family giving up all hope.
summary.zh: 兩獵手的妹妹某日一去不返；再現時兜帽之下竟孕育著會咬唇吮血的蟲怪，並自陳『嫁的丈夫非人類』。兄弟們攻入谷中大屋，撕碎其後代，又以弓矛射殺如屋牆般巨大、盤繞其身的丈夫，並誡她勿再犯舊習。然而她掌中一條黑紋小蟲日漸長大，最後她再度消失；母親死於尋女途中，一個兄弟折了腿——全家從此放棄希望。

sensitivity.note: Animal-husband and monstrous-offspring motifs; graphic violence recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: An old woman lived with her three children, two sons and a daughter. The sons were good hunters and loved their sister exceedingly; as time passed on the mother observed a change in her daughter's manners, and one day the daughter went out by herself and stayed away for good. The brothers sought her far and wide, gave it up at last, and again took to kayaking and hunting, living alone with their mother. One day, when she was all by herself, lying on the ledge beneath the skin coverlet, she remarked a thing like a shadow gliding across the doorway, and turning that way beheld her long-lost daughter; perceiving the amowt (hood) she wore, she asked her to come and sit beside her, admiring her beautiful clothes, the amowt particularly, made of soft and thin reindeer-skin. When a low cry was heard from within it, the mother asked her to take out the little one she was carrying to let her see it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughter answered her, 'What I carry on my back is no human being. Thou hadst better hide thyself beneath thy skin coverlet.' The mother did so, but peeping through a small opening, was dreadfully alarmed at seeing her daughter produce a large reptile, which she allowed to bite her lips so as to make them bleed; having caressed it in a motherly way, she let it suck at her breast, then replaced it in her amowt and asked her mother to look up again. 'Where is thy dwelling-place, child?' 'My house lies far from here, in a very large valley; but my husband is not of human race: so none of you must ever think of coming to see me,' she added, and left. In the evening, when the sons returned, the mother told them what had happened: 'I have seen your sister, but in a very low and contemptible state. Only think! she carried a vile reptile in her amowt, and was also married to such a one!' The brothers got into a great rage, prepared their bows and arrows to attack the vermin, and starting together soon found the great house in the valley.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After a careful inspection of all the mountains they ventured to peep through the window, and saw their sister comfortably seated in a snug and well-furnished room. They entered at once, killed her offspring, and having torn it to pieces, threw it outside. They did not leave their sorrowing sister during the day-time; but towards evening they saw her dreadful husband approaching from some remote part of the country — its size like the wall of a house, in its mouth a large reindeer. When it came nearer the brothers went out to hide at the back of the house, whence they saw the reptile drop the reindeer on the ground and afterwards enter the house; peeping again, they saw the creature twining itself closely round the body of their sister, so that only the tuft of her hair was visible. They tightened the strings of their bows, keeping them ready bent, then made a little noise to alarm the beast: the instant it emerged from the house it was aimed at from both sides, and when all their arrows had been spent, finished off and killed with their spears. They made for home bringing their sister along, as well as all her things and some dried reindeer; and the sister was once more with her parents, who warned her to leave off her former bad habits. After a little her manner towards them again suddenly changed; they perceived she was always carrying something about in her hand — a small worm or reptile with black streaks round its body. Every day it grew in size, so that before long both sides appeared out of her hand; and now she disappeared a second time. The brothers again went in search of her, this time taking their mother along; but she soon died on her way, one brother had his leg broken, and henceforth they gave up all hope of ever finding their sister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.

title.en: Angutisugsuk: The Bewitched Wall and the Brother's Spear
title.zh: 安古提舒克：被咒的牆與兄弟之矛

region.en: Winter quarters at the fiord, Greenland

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two offended old men bewitch the empty house-wall to sow discord in the family of three hunter-brothers. The charm works: a wooden plate and spoon promised for mending a jacket sets wife against wife, brother against brother, until Angutisugsuk lames his own brother and flees with the unloved wife, returning again and again to kill him. Ambushed at last through an old man's hand-omen spell, he is hamstrung, speared in the shoulder, and dies on the beach — and the mournful cry goes up, 'Alas! we have killed him who did well towards us,' the wronged second wife put to death in his place.
summary.zh: 兩名懷恨的老人對空屋的牆壁施咒，播下猜忌。咒術應驗：一隻木盤木勺引發兩妻相爭、兄弟相殘——安古提舒克打瘸親弟，攜不受寵的次妻出走，又屢屢返回謀殺胞弟。老人以手背朝下之兆施咒設伏，他終被縛住腳筋、肩上連中數矛，倒斃海灘——眾人哀嘆『唉！我們殺了待我們那麼好的人』；肇事的次妻亦被處死陪葬。

sensitivity.note: Sorcery-by-proxy (bewitching a house) is a documented Greenlandic belief. Killing of the wife recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There were three brothers, the eldest called Angutisugsuk, who had never lived apart, all clever hunters, especially Angutisugsuk. One winter the weather was dreadfully severe and all the neighbours in great want; only the three brothers had enough to spare, and the others claimed their assistance. Two old men came to them with that intention, and during their visit the wife of Angutisugsuk remonstrated that they were having rather too many visitors, at which the old men quickly took offence. In spring, when Angutisugsuk's family left their winter-quarters on a long excursion, they visited the place in their kayaks, entered the empty house, and practised all manner of sorcery and witchcraft upon the wall adjoining the ledge occupied by Angutisugsuk's wife, in order to produce discord among the family when they came back from their travels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In autumn they all returned to the old house as usual. One day Angutisugsuk stayed home to make a wooden plate and spoon; he had got two wives, both clever at needle-work, and offered to give her who would mend his fur jacket the plate and spoon. The first wife answered before the second could put in a word — 'I want to have them — I will mend the jacket' — and worked very quickly; but the second wife, the best beloved, became envious and got into a passion. Perceiving this, the husband struck her, because of her having borne him no children; at this his youngest son began crying, and seeing it, the child's uncle fell upon the father, who was still ill-treating his second wife. In this fight Angutisugsuk thrust his brother against the door-sill with such force that his thigh-bone was bruised, and would have followed up his advantage but for the younger brother and some others who interfered. Thus it came to pass as the old men had planned when they went and bewitched the empty house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Having lamed his brother, Angutisugsuk next day loaded his boat and went off, taking a small roofless house a little north of his former station, making a shift with his tent-poles for roof-beams; his proper wife he left behind, taking only the second one. Seeing his brother was now able to stir, he resolved to kill him, and repeatedly returned to despatch him, but always found his younger brother or his nephew by his side — these two watching the sick man by turns, only one at a time going out in his kayak. Encountering his nephew at sea he resolved to pursue him, but as soon as they came within sight of the house on shore he left off and turned back. The invalid bade his son ask the neighbours to assist in getting Angutisugsuk out of the way, 'because he has gone raving mad; but two or three men will not suffice, for he is immensely strong himself.' The son brought a considerable party of kayakers, who hid their kayaks behind the house for the night; early in the morning they saw Angutisugsuk emerging from behind a rocky point, and an old man among the strangers drew his hood closer and pronounced a magic spell, adding that if it were likely to succeed, Angutisugsuk as a sure sign would turn the backs of his hands downwards instead of using the palms in ascending the beach. Watching him closely, they noticed he did as foretold, and no longer had any doubt of their success.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He drew his kayak only half-way out of the water, went straight up to the house as if to enter at once, then bethinking himself of something turned back to the large boat for a flensing-knife and proceeded to the entry. The men reclined on the side-ledge couches except two posted at the inner entrance ready to seize him. Seeing his brother on the main ledge, he addressed him: 'Here is a brave man for thee! I'll show thee the way to fight! Didst thou really believe I did not intend to kill thee?' — and advancing a step or two was soon seized by the two men and quickly disarmed. Conducted outside, all the rest fell upon him, but nobody could manage to overthrow him; at last, hamstrung, he fell, and they held a council as to which of them should first stab him. The invalid brother was carried out to finish him off, put down close beside him, had his spear fetched from under the boat, and lanced his brother several times in the shoulder: 'Now let go your hold; if he boasts himself a man, he will be sure to rise.' He did get up and went towards his kayak on the beach, but fell down dead before he reached it. Then the surviving brother exclaimed, 'Alas! we have killed him who did well towards us. In the short, dark days, when we were almost starving, he did not mind toiling away for us. I am sorry indeed: now do kill me also!' He asked his brother, his son, and all the other men; finding nobody would do it, he said, 'Well, then, go and fetch his second wife, and kill her at any rate; it was she who began it all.' They did so; the person who slew her admonished the bystanders to put together all her things, all her clothes, jackets of reindeer-skin, breeches and boots of seal-skin, carry them along with her, close up the burial-place well, and heap plenty of stones on top of it. Later on, when the invalid recovered, he felt great remorse for his act of violence; but the old magician was quite satisfied that Angutisugsuk should have been killed by his brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.

title.en: Sitliamat: The Bear That Pushed Them Home
title.zh: 西特利阿馬特：推冰送歸的熊

region.en: Drift-ice and the unknown other shore

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; abridged text, resembling tales 16 and 19, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Storm-driven onto an unknown shore, three brothers and their companion shelter with an old couple whose pale, weaponless son recovers among them. At parting the old man dives into the sea as a bear: gull-amulet men glide on the waves' surface, the raven-amulet companion sinks and is left behind, and the bear shoulders their iceberg home with the warning to shut their eyes — landing them south of their old habitation, where boys play who were named in memory of them. Their lost wives remarried are restored, and in winter a bald-headed bear is feasted with entire seals at the entrance and vanishes forever into the sea.
summary.zh: 風暴把三兄弟拋上異鄉海岸；一對老夫婦收留他們，其慘白的無器之子也漸漸康復。臨別時老人躍海化熊：護身符為海鷗者踏浪滑行，渡鴉護符的同伴沉底被留，熊以肩推冰山送他們閉眼歸鄉——上岸處男孩們正以他們的名字玩耍。被再嫁的妻子們歸還原夫；冬日一頭白首之熊登岸受整豹之宴，飽食後循跡入海，從此絕跡。

sensitivity.note: Amulet-bird (gull vs raven) as homecoming fate; bald-headed bear gratitude motif. Parallel transformation endings to tale 16 (Tiggak).

passages.text: There were three brothers, the eldest named Sitliarnat, who one day all went out hunting on the frozen sea, accompanied by a person in no way related to them. All of a sudden a south-east storm arose, the ice creaked and gave way beneath their feet, and nothing remained but to mount an iceberg; having got there, they drifted far away out on the great ocean, nearly starving with hunger when they at length touched upon an unknown shore and landed. Roaming about in search of people, they passed an isthmus on which they observed a little hut with only one window. Sitliarnat spoke: 'Let them make me their first prize' — and crossed the threshold in front of his companions. Inside they found only an old couple, the sole inhabitants; the four strangers seated themselves on the ledge, and nobody spoke until the old man, eyeing them more closely and breathing upon them, asked, 'Whence do you come?' 'Some time ago we set off from the land on the other side of the ocean, and went out on the ice to catch seals; but a gale from the south-east came on, breaking up the ice and drifting us across to your country. So here we are; three of us are brothers, and the fourth is a companion of ours.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'After travelling so far people are apt to get hungry,' the old man observed to his wife, adding words the people did not understand; she fetched some blubber in a pan, boiled it, and served it in a wooden dish — though almost fainting with hunger, they only tasted a very little of it, and soon after a proper meal was set before them. 'Our only provider is staying away a long time; we have been expecting him back this last month. He left us to go out hunting, and has not yet returned; we are much afraid he may have encountered some wicked people and have come to grief.' The visitors began to think, 'What sort of people may these be?' — but stayed on, the old man providing food for some time. One morning they heard a voice calling from without, 'I want to get in; do let me get in!' — the old man returned holding his son by the hand, very pale and haggard, who lay on the side ledge for several days until one morning he rose up very early, recovered in health, strength, appetite, and aspect, and took up his task as provider — strange to say, never seen to carry any weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The visitors prolonged their stay for several years. One evening the old man questioned the eldest brother, 'What did they give thee for thy amulet when thou wert born?' 'In my infancy I got a carrion-gull, one of those that always seek the carrion farthest out to sea.' 'So thou mayst be sure of returning to thy own country at some time or other.' All the brothers had the same bird; but the companion's was a raven, a bird that always seeks his prey landward — 'I doubt if thou wilt ever see thy country again, if it is so.' The old man used to rise the earliest of them all, seen on some mountain-top marking the state of the air and the weather, and one day entered with the remark, 'When the wind goes down and the weather gets settled, I shall take you across' — they wondered, there being no ice, neither boats nor kayaks, and they did not even know in what direction their country was situated. One morning while they were still fast asleep he cried, 'It is no time for sleeping now. Make haste and get up, if ye really long for your homes; I shall see you along myself' — and following him down to the steep shore where they had landed years ago: 'Now watch me!' Taking a run he leapt into the sea, dived down, and reappeared in the shape of a bear: 'If Sitliarnat really has a gull for his amulet, it will soon appear to him. Do as I have done, and throw thyself into the water.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Sitliarnat still lingered a little, but the bear went on, 'If thou dost not follow me into the ocean, thou wilt never get home.' He ran on and took the leap; as soon as he had plunged down he again rose, merely touching the surface with his feet, gliding along as if on solid ice instead of on the waves of the sea — and the gull also made its appearance, a large iceberg seen which he climbed, both his brothers following. The old man turned to the fourth: 'Thou, too, wouldst like to return, I know; now try thy wings!' He plunged into the sea trying to fly, but went right down, and would have lost breath but for the bear, who put him on shore: 'No, thou wilt never get home, because thou hast got a raven for thy amulet; thou canst return to my house as before.' The bear spoke to the three: 'Shut your eyes and sit close together. If ye open your eyes, ye will never get home. I shall now put my shoulder to the iceberg, and push you away.' Their place of refuge began to shake beneath them, and they had started on their journey, moving onwards until they felt a quake as if touching something hard. 'Open your eyes' — they beheld a country spreading before them and recognised it as their own, landed just a little south of their former habitation. They asked the bear to enter, that they might recompense him in some way; but he said, 'No, I don't care for being paid — I merely intended to do you a good turn; but when in winter-time ye should happen to see a bear with a bald head, and your companions prepare to hunt him down, then try to make them desist, and put some food before him' — and plunging into the sea he instantly disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers went up to their former house and knew it to be inhabited because of little boys seen at play outside, named after them by their parents in remembrance of their lost friends. Their wives had all married again, but the other relatives rejoiced greatly at receiving those they had given up for lost. Asked about their companion, they answered they had left him 'on the opposite shore.' Perceiving that the husbands of their former wives feared them, they reassured them — 'We don't intend any harm towards you. Many thanks to you that ye have provided so well for our relatives' — but the wives, nevertheless, were given back to them. During the winter the bear was almost forgotten, till one evening when they were all at home some of the men exclaimed, 'A bear is making for the shore!' Collecting their arms, the brothers interfered, crying, 'Just wait a little; we must first have a look at him' — and instantly recognised their own bear: 'Without his good aid we should never have reached home again. Don't hunt that bear; make haste and give him a feast.' When the bear had got on shore he went right up to the house, sat down on his haunches before the entrance, head turned towards it; the people put several entire seals before him and beckoned him to eat, all the men gathered round him. When the meal was ended the bear lay down to sleep while the children played round him; after a while he awoke, having eaten a little more, arose, and following his own traces back to the beach, leapt into the sea, and was never seen any more. It is said that the descendants of Sitliarnat were very prosperous and multiplied greatly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Reindeer-Hunt of Merkisalik: The Bewitched Knuckle
title.zh: 梅基薩利克的獵鹿記：被咒的指骨

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from two copies (one North Greenland, before 1828), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Visiting hunters mock the lone son of old Merkisalik — 'There must be any amount of animals in this place, since even Merkisalik's son is capable of getting at them' — and give him the last loophole. He alarms the herd, runs down the leaders over the hills, and returns cool and refreshed to their red-faced wrath. But the father of the visitors asks for a knuckle 'for a gimlet,' bewitches the knee-joint, and the swelling kills the son; Merkisalik makes a tupilak of whitened bones until it takes the shape of a little whale, and the hunters' sons vanish one by one from the north, harpooning 'a little whale,' until his wrath is somewhat appeased.
summary.zh: 造訪的獵隊譏誚梅基薩利克的獨子，逼他守最後一個射孔；他驚散鹿群、追過山脊，衣冠整齊地涼快而歸，令敵人紅著臉無言。然而仇家之父討走一根指骨『做手鑽』，暗中詛咒其膝關節——腫瘤日漸奪去兒子性命。老人以漂白的獸骨捏製圖皮拉克，直到它化作小鯨之形；此後北方的仇家子弟一個個『叉中小鯨』而消失，老人胸中恨意方才稍平。

sensitivity.note: Bewitched-gift motif (the requested knuckle as carrier of sorcery); tupilak-making as revenge, as in tale 13. Deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Merkisalik had only one son to assist him in providing for his family; in the summer they always hunted along the shores of the same fiord without other company. Growing old and infirm, Merkisalik gave up hunting and left the providing to his son. Once, taken up at the fiord again with the son out hunting, the old people were left by themselves expecting no visitors — when they suddenly observed a boat sailing up the inlet right before the wind, accompanied by several kayakers. Merkisalik was much pleased, and ordered his wife to put out some dry meat for a bite on landing, rejoicing that his son should henceforth have companions on his hunting excursions. Among the visitors were a great number of men, some old and rather talkative and entertaining; the son returning from the mountains was likewise very glad of the company, treated them with the utmost hospitality, and invited them to the meal as soon as it was boiled and ready. They conversed very politely, and soon agreed in going out together the next day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before long they came in sight of a number of animals feeding on the grass down in the valleys. The drivers were sent out, the hunters made walls of earth furnished with loopholes, and the visitors proposed that Merkisalik's son should be the last to shoot — he agreed; but when the drivers had surrounded the animals and began to drive them towards the loopholed walls, the thought struck him, 'What if they are too greedy to leave me any chance at all?' The others took aim and shot all that were to be got; he assisted in stripping off the skins, remaining a little behind on descending the hills towards the tents. At supper one of the men remarked, 'There must be any amount of animals in this place, since even Merkisalik's son is capable of getting at them.' The Merkisaliks heard the slight in silence; afterwards, sitting together in their own tent, the father said, 'It can't be otherwise; we must just let them have their way, seeing that they are so many.' The next day was spent in the same manner, the son allowed to take up his position as far away as possible from the drivers; the man who had scorned him spoke to him in a similar fashion again, at which he got into a great passion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They set out together the next day to the entrance of a great valley almost overcrowded with reindeer, and as before ordered him to choose his hiding-place and make his loophole behind them all — at which he murmured to himself, 'If this is to go on, I shall never be able to get anything. I think I will give the beasts the alarm, that they may all run away.' When the flock approached, driven by the drivers, he feigned to be busy about something, was warned to be quiet, stopped a moment, and began to move about again. All of a sudden the leader stopped short, turned round, and bounded off as fast as possible; the others began to follow but dropped short one after another, so that at the other end of the valley but one had kept up with him, and that one soon tired out. Merkisalik's son disappeared on the other side of the hills, pursuing the fast-running animals. Slowly the men followed his traces; from the top of the hill they beheld numbers of deer with white bellies ready killed in the valley on the other side, and on a stone close by the huntsman seated, already quite cool and refreshed. The others arrived, faces all red with heat and wrath, and nobody spoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They set to work stripping the deer; while the others finished one, he stripped and cut up two, and packing his bundle said, 'Ye may all of you take as much as ye like.' The man who had formerly ridiculed him became quite mute and would not join the rest. Merkisalik's son got home first with his burden on his back; when the others came without anything, the Merkisaliks had all their pots and pans on the fire, and, after their wont, invited the foreigners to join them — but during the meal the host tried in vain to begin a conversation; all remained mute, and even their old father kept silent. Having done eating they retired, excepting the father, who now began to be a little talkative and, as if by chance, remarked, 'We want something that would do for a gimlet; would ye mind letting me have that knuckle?' Merkisalik gave it willingly: 'We have got lots of them.' The following morning the Merkisaliks were aroused by a clattering noise of poles — the visitors pulling down their tent and preparing to depart — and they were once more alone, the son again hunting by himself. One day, busy bringing down the deer he had stalked, he told them he had got a swelling at his knee; it grew in size, getting worse and worse, and at length he died — but not till he had made known to them that his disease was solely caused by the father of their former visitors, who, in order to hurt him, had bewitched the knee-joint he had asked of them, which had worked back upon him and killed him. The poor old people were inconsolable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was now autumn; the little lakes began to be covered with ice, and it was time to leave the inland country for the sea-coast. They first wept at the tomb of their son, and, still wailing and complaining, went down the firth with a light easterly breeze. Having arrived at their winter-quarters, Merkisalik's mind was filled with hatred, always contemplating revenge: to carry it out he resolved to make a tupilak to destroy his enemies. Every day he collected bones of all sorts of animals, put them into the brook close by to whiten, then mixed them up with hairs taken from boat-skins; when he had got as many as he required, he made them alive and put them into the brook which flowed on to the sea. Watching the tupilak, he saw it taking the shape of an agpaliarsuk, which dived down and turned round to its owner; but he said, 'Thou art not the thing I want thee to be yet.' Instantly it dived and reappeared in the shape of a dovekie — 'That won't do neither.' It underwent many changes, taking the shape of all sorts of birds, then of all manner of seals and dolphins; at last, after another dive, its breath was heard like a mighty roar, and he beheld a small whale — 'This will do; thou shalt avenge us.' 'Where am I to go?' the animal seemed to inquire. 'To the hunting place of the many brothers' — it took one long breath, dived down into the sea, and the man returned home to bide his time. One evening a kayaker appeared rounding the northern point — a poor relative and very old man, quartered at the same place as their former visitors — who related: 'Some days ago an accident occurred up at our place; one of the many brothers has not returned home. The day before his departure he told us that he had harpooned a little whale, adding that he would now go out in search of it; but he has never yet returned.' The maker of the tupilak feigned compassion, but inwardly rejoiced. Again and again the old visitor returned, reporting 'Yesterday the same accident happened to another of the brothers' — and at last that the last of the brothers had now disappeared, the poor parents very much grieved because of their bereavement. On hearing this, Merkisalik's wrath was somewhat appeased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.

title.en: Namak: The Sling of the Avenger
title.zh: 納馬克：復仇者的投石索

region.en: North Greenland winter-house and northern enemy station
region.zh: 北格陵蘭冬屋與北方仇敵營地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; single manuscript written down in North Greenland before 1828, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 25 'Namak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Orphaned when house-fellows killed both his parents, Namak is adopted by a foster-father who worries and provokes him on purpose — 'Namak, thy enemies have come to kill thee, too' — and gives him not a kayak but a sling. Cheated too often to stir, he rises only when he hears the tents clattering for real: lifting a thong-seal one-handed to cut his sling, he ambushes on the beach and sinks three boats with thrown stones, crews and all, his mind at rest. Years later father and son row to the enemy's northern station, tear the walrus-tooth pulling-thong with one hand, and out-pull the whole house, arms hooked one after another — never invited again.
summary.zh: 父母被同屋人殺害的孤兒納馬克，被一個故意激將的養父收養——『納馬克，敵人來殺你了』——給他的不是皮艇而是投石索。被騙多次的他直到親耳聽見拆帳聲才行動：單手翻轉長鬚海豹割取投石索，伏於石堆間，三塊飛石擊沉三艘敵船連人帶舟——心境自此安寧。多年後父子北訪仇敵，徒手扯斷鑲海象牙的拉繩，又逐一勾臂角力，無人能撼其分毫——仇人從此再不敢相邀。

sensitivity.note: The native writer's note (quoted by Rink): before Christianity strong men abounded because bad consciences induced them to cultivate strength — recorded here as part of the source. Boat-sinking killings recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: The parents of Namak were both killed by their house-fellows; while he was yet a weak and helpless child, a man happened to take pity on him and adopted him for his son. But this same foster-father was fond of worrying the boy, and inventing stories to frighten and excite him: sometimes, when the child was asleep, he would cry out, 'Namak, thy enemies have come to kill thee, too' — at first much alarmed, by degrees he got used to it. Sometimes the foster-father would say, 'Ah, how forgetful that Namak is! Here are his parents newly murdered, and he forgetting all about it' — at this Namak would get into a great rage. While still a child, his father one day made him a present of a sling, saying, 'I don't mean to give thee a kayak, because I believe that thy enemies will kill thee for all that; but take this sling and practise with it.' Namak instantly began, and soon got very clever in using it; in spring he would betake himself to solitary places, practising his sling, always pondering over the things his foster-father had said to stir up vengeance within him. At home he spoke little, but inwardly rejoiced at his growing strength; sometimes he brought in hares, sometimes ptarmigan, got entirely by means of his sling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the summer he never slept at night, but always in the day-time. Sometimes, when he had gone to sleep, his father would bring home a seal, and he was then awakened to assist in carrying it up to the house; he would then hide his strength, making-believe it was very hard work for him. One day, however, he said that his sling was too weak, and his father went to cut him a stronger one out of a very thick piece of seal-skin — after that time he left off gibing the boy, because he began to fear him. During the winter it was reported that the enemies of Namak intended to remove farther to the north in spring; he got quite enraged at the thought that they would be going away before he could be revenged, and from that day his manner changed altogether. When spring came round and they left their winter-house for the tents, he one day said, 'I wish I could get myself a new sling' — the father went out in his kayak and had the good luck to catch a thong-seal, brought in while Namak was still asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the women were busy flensing it and preparing the skin for boat-covers, the husband said, 'It just occurs to me that Namak is wanting a sling,' then roused him: 'Namak, thy enemies are making ready to depart.' He awoke and ran out, standing staring at the neighbours; on his way down to the beach his foster-father said to him, 'Just cut out a line for thy sling, wherever thou choosest.' Keeping an eye on his neighbours, he took the knife from his father, lifted up the seal by one of the forepaws with only one hand, and turning it over without any difficulty, cut himself a sling to his liking, all in one piece — on seeing this his foster-father got quite frightened. Some time after, their neighbours were really going to depart. Namak slept, and his father roused him: 'Namak, this time thou mayst believe me; thy enemies are in the very act of departing' — but Namak did not think fit to stir; he had been cheated too often. 'Now they are taking their tents away' — and as he himself could hear the clattering of the bars and poles, he rose and put on jacket and boots, but without getting into the sleeves of his jacket, and catching hold of his sling from under the ledge, hid it inside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Further down on the beach were some large stone-heaps; there he lay in ambush, and now that he had determined to revenge himself, no more concealed his strength. While some were yet bringing down their luggage, the first boat put out, rowing briskly, and when right athwart of him Namak put a big stone in his sling and threw it into the boat, where it made a large hole, so that it instantly began to sink — 'Alas! alas!' The other boat hurried on to rescue them, but underwent the same fate; the third tried to save itself by turning in time, but at that instant he flung the stone at it, hitting the prow and cleaving right through — and thus he destroyed three boats, crews and all, and his mind now got rest. One boat was saved from destruction, having gone out to sea at once instead of keeping along the shore. His enemies increased in number after they had established themselves somewhere in the north, and seeing they had reason to fear him, trained themselves to be as vigorous as he. Namak married, and though he had never had a kayak himself, taught his son to practise kayak-paddling; the son grew up an excellent kayaker and owned a boat as well as a tent. Reports reached them that their enemies were numerous and strong; at last he persuaded his son to go and look them up, and in spring they went northward in their boat, asking the people they met, 'Where are Namak's enemies?' — 'Farther north' was the constant answer. Learning that the station was close at hand, they rowed on incessantly instead of landing in the evening to take rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On arrival they asked the people who came down to the beach to meet them, 'Where are Namak's enemies?' — but these made no reply, entering their houses, and the travellers had to make their way on shore by themselves; neither were they afterwards invited to visit. They took up their winter-quarters at that very place; in the beginning Namak advised his son to watch them closely, afterwards they got less suspicious. That same winter, one morning, it blew a gale from the south-west and the kayakers remained at home; on that day it was announced, 'They all want to see Namak' — ready in a moment, the son likewise going: thus they were going to visit their enemies for the first time. There was only set forth meat for two; the son did not taste much of it, but the father continued eating till the dish was nearly emptied. The visitors did not speak; at length one of the other party proposed different sports, saying, 'Ye ought to try strength at the pulling-thong first' — he took out the string fitted with walrus-teeth from beneath the ledge and threw it upon the skin spread on the floor for the champions. But Namak said, 'This is but child's-play for people who really want to try a match' — and so saying, took hold of and tore the thong asunder with one hand, then flung them down on the floor. Another offered to try strength with him, hooking their arms together and trying to pull each other over; Namak did not hesitate but at once sat down on the skin, and they tried one after another, nobody able to move his arm in the least. Seeing that they were not able to match him, they all departed. The son went home, but Namak never stirred but stayed on; at last he prepared to put on his outer coat, very slowly and deliberately, always expecting an attack. They were never invited afterwards. In spring they again wanted to go to the south, and at parting he let his house-fellows first go into the boat while he kept back, still expecting an attack from his enemies; but seeing that they did not come, he finally left the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.
